newsitem.title: UK: Buoyant dollar closes off best levels in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant dollar closes off best levels in Europe.

text.p: The dollar closed more than a pfennig higher in Europe but off its peak after short-term profit-taking set in on its rise above 1.63 marks for the first time since June 1994, traders said.
Another assault on the mark on its European crosses provided the dollar with the fuel to motor further.

"The mark came under intense pressure in Europe, which gave added impetus to the firm dollar," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London. "After such a rally it's due for a bit of a setback."

The dollar jumped against a range of European currencies, breaking through 1.42 against the Swiss franc and 5.50 against the French franc for the first time since summer 1994. But U.S. foreign exchange desks were thinly staffed due to Martin Luther King Day in the U.S., prompting short-term traders to take profits.
At 1604 GMT, the dollar was at 1.6235/45 marks, off its 1.6315 high but well above 1.6112/22 in late European trade on Friday.
Dollar/yen was at 117.92/118.02 after rising to a fresh 46-month high at 118.29. It was up from 117.05/15 in late European trading on Friday.

Expectations of healthy GDP growth in the last quarter of 1996 and other rosy economic prospects for the United States combined with weakness in Japan and Germany meant there was little to stop the dollar from stretching to new heights.

"There isn't any alteration to the underlying trend," said Brian Martin, chief economist forex at BZW in London. "The background to the dollar is increasingly positive." The U.S. currency is likely to remain well supported on dips below 1.62 marks, traders said.
"I wouldn't advise 'be long of dollars' any more but there is no reason to go short either," said Norfield at ABN Amro.
The Finnish markka and Italian lira broke the upper limits of their notional 2.25-percent upper limit in the ERM.
The assault on the mark was led by the Norwegian crown, which made a new 52-month high of 3.8955 per mark, as speculative funds continued to pour into the currency, traders said.
The markka followed suit, leaping to 2.8990 per mark, a level not seen since September 1992, after the break of the notional 2.25-percent limit at around 2.97 sparked panic mark sales.
The markka and the lira, which joined the ERM in autumn 1996, are allowed to fluctuate by 15 percent within their ERM bands. Their central rates are 3.04 markka and 990 lire, respectively.
The cross pushed above 2.70 marks but was off its 2.7065 mark peak in late trade at 2.7005/15, while cable dropped almost a full cent to $1.6612/19 from $1.6702/12 in late trade on Friday.
